title: Season 1: The Room Decides
subtitle: A season where the plan broke more often than it held, and Misha won by being useful to every side until the final question.

winner.name: Misha
winner.keyStats: Misha won with 2 HOH wins, 4 veto wins, 3 wins under threat, 3 nominations, 3 times pulled off the block, zero eviction votes against, and a 5–4 jury vote over Jules.
winner.strategy: Misha’s winning game was not clean control; it was durable positioning. She moved between structures, kept enough personal bonds alive to survive danger, and converted late comp wins into the only choices that mattered. Her best work was making people believe she was an available number even when she was quietly choosing which room survived the week.
winner.legacy: Misha becomes the first winner as the season’s best hybrid: socially insulated enough to be saved, competitive enough to save herself, and ruthless enough to cut Joel at final three. The win is narrow, but it is not accidental.

placements.name: Misha
placements.notes: Misha won because she combined late competition leverage with enough social debt to survive the weeks where she should have been exposed.
placements.story: Misha’s game was built on being included without always being identified as the person deciding. Early on, she attached herself to Hasan and the larger Power Couple structure, then survived its collapse by keeping individual bonds alive with Jules, Dylon, and later the jury. The record matters here: three times on the block, three times pulled down, and zero eviction votes against is not passive luck; it is proof that people with power kept finding reasons to protect her. Her weakness was jury management, especially when her answers at finale sometimes dodged the question, but her overall arc had more agency than the edit always made obvious. The key stretch is the endgame, where she wins HOH and veto at the exact moments that prevent Joel or Tobias from dictating the finish. Cutting Joel at final three was the correct winning move, even if it nearly cost her his vote.
keyMoments: Week 3: joins the expanding Power Couple structure while also building a separate bond with Hasan
Week 5: helps flip the close Hasan/Zella vote and owns the move when pressed
Week 10: wins veto on the block and forces Jules to renom Natasha
Week 13: wins HOH and nominates Jane, Gyselle and Joel, setting up the Gyselle eviction
Week 14: wins HOH and veto, keeping full control of the Jane/Tobias block
Week 15: wins veto under threat, saves herself, and casts the sole vote to evict Tobias
Finale: wins Part 1 and Part 3 of the final HOH, then cuts Joel for Jules
placements.resume: Misha could argue that she won six competitions, survived three nominations without ever receiving an eviction vote, was saved by others three times because of relationships she built, and made the final decision to remove Joel, the finalist she believed could beat her.
placements.demise: Misha’s last real threat was Joel winning the final HOH or being taken to the end. That threat died when Misha beat Joel in the jury statements tiebreaker and chose Jules instead, turning the most dangerous endgame opponent into the final juror.
placements.optimalLine: Her correct line was exactly what she did: prioritize survival over ownership until the jury was seated, then win late and cut Joel. The only improvement was cleaner final answers to Felipe, Gyselle, Aaron, and Tobias.

placements.name: Jules
placements.notes: Jules played the best losing game: deeply connected, strategically present, and one jury vote short because too many jurors saw comfort without enough ownership.
placements.story: Jules was in the season’s machinery from the first real vote and stayed there by being the person people could talk to when the room was shifting. His 78% voting alignment and five groups with nine people show a player who was usually close to the decision, not dragged behind it. He survived being the target four times, which is a real finalist résumé even without dominant veto numbers. His HOH weeks were meaningful, especially the Ireland eviction setup, but the jury split exposed the flaw: many relationships felt real, but not all jurors believed the moves were his. Taking Misha to the end was not his choice, but his relationship with her is why she chose him over Joel. He lost because his social game was strong enough to reach the end and just short of strong enough to beat the winner.
keyMoments: Week 2: survives the block beside Stella after the house chooses Stella 10–3
Week 4: wins HOH and veto, nominates Harriett, Natasha and Ireland, and leaves nominations intact
Week 8: helps redirect the Nico vote after Dylon’s veto forces a renom
Week 10: wins HOH, nominates Jane, Misha and Ireland, and later renoms Natasha
Week 12: survives the Felipe vote 3–2 after Gyselle wins Block Buster
Week 15: survives Misha’s sole vote when Tobias is evicted instead
Finale: receives four jury votes and loses 5–4
placements.resume: Jules could argue he survived four target nominations, won two HOHs and a veto, maintained overlapping endgame bonds with Misha, Joel, Tobias, Gyselle and Felipe, and was trusted enough that Misha chose him over Joel at final three.
placements.demise: Jules lost at the jury phase, not in the final HOH. Misha’s competition résumé and her ownership at the reunion converted Dylon, Ireland, Natasha, Gyselle and Aaron, while Jules’s best relationships produced only four votes.
placements.optimalLine: Jules needed to claim more of the votes he shaped before finale night. At the time, his quieter approach kept him alive, so the mistake was not the path; it was arriving at final speeches without enough clean ownership.

placements.name: Joel
placements.notes: Joel had the comp record and endgame gravity to win, but he lost the season when Misha correctly refused to sit beside him.
placements.story: Joel’s game was powerful but jagged. Three HOHs, three vetoes, and two wins under threat made him impossible to ignore, and his later weeks forced everyone to plan around him. He was also blindsided three times and only voted with the house 75%, which shows he was not always in the room when the decision became final. His best stretch came from Week 11 onward, when his HOH, veto and social pairing with Felipe made him a central endgame figure. The problem was that his win equity became too obvious. By final three, both Misha and Jules knew Joel was the person the jury could reward for a visible résumé, and Misha took the only path that denied him the chairs.
keyMoments: Week 2: wins veto and removes himself, forcing Zella onto the block
Week 7: wins HOH and nominates Dylon, Jane and Ireland
Week 11: wins HOH and veto, leaves nominations intact, then breaks the tie to evict Natasha
Week 13: wins veto under threat and saves himself from Misha’s block
Week 15: wins HOH at final four and nominates Misha and Jules
Finale: wins Part 2 but loses Part 3 to Misha on the tiebreaker
Finale: is cut at final three when Misha chooses Jules
placements.resume: Joel could argue six total HOH/veto wins, multiple late-game saves, a tie-breaking eviction of Natasha, and a final-four HOH that forced Misha to win veto or leave.
placements.demise: Misha ended Joel by beating him in Part 3 of the final HOH and choosing Jules. It became inevitable once Joel’s résumé and jury upside were obvious enough that sitting beside him looked like choosing second place.
placements.optimalLine: Joel’s best available line was to take Misha out at final four or make Jules believe Joel was easier to beat than Misha. He did not have enough control once Misha won final veto and then final HOH.

placements.name: Tobias
placements.notes: Tobias was one of the season’s best social-position players, but repeated pawn exposure eventually made him expendable at final four.
placements.story: Tobias’s finish understates the game. He was in six groups with a reach of ten people and voted with the house 82%, which means he was usually close to where the vote actually landed. He survived five nominations, mostly as pawn or renom, and that is both a compliment and the warning sign: people trusted him enough to use him, then trusted themselves enough to cut him. His best strategic work was in the Dylon eviction and in staying socially relevant through multiple broken structures. His weakness was that he kept too many final-two relationships soft instead of locking a winning route. At final four, Misha held veto and the only vote, and Tobias had no way to make himself more useful than Jules.
keyMoments: Week 1: wins the first HOH, gaining early position despite no eviction
Week 2: votes out Stella despite a prior endgame promise
Week 9: helps make Dylon the unanimous boot after previously being tied to him
Week 11: survives the tied Natasha vote when Joel breaks the tie
Week 14: survives beside Jane 2–0 after Misha leaves nominations intact
Week 15: lands on the block after Misha uses veto and is evicted by Misha’s sole vote
placements.resume: Tobias could argue he survived five blocks, maintained the widest relationship spread in the house, helped move the Dylon vote, and was trusted as a number by almost every major structure at some point.
placements.demise: Misha ended Tobias at final four. Once Misha won veto, Joel had to nominate Tobias as the replacement, and Misha chose to keep Jules, honoring the relationship that gave her the best final two odds.
placements.optimalLine: Tobias needed to treat Misha as the late-game threat earlier, not as a flexible emotional bond. Once she had veto at final four, his best pitch was real but structurally too late.

placements.name: Jane
placements.notes: Jane returned from the battle back and played a sharp late social game, but her safety depended on other people choosing not to finish moves they had already started.
placements.story: Jane’s game is unusual because she entered as a separate houseguest after the twins twist and then re-entered again through the Battle Back. Her best work came after that return, when she rebuilt trust with Gyselle, Tobias and Joel and briefly became a real vote broker. She won an HOH and a veto, used the veto on Joel, and had enough social credibility that several players were nervous about sitting next to her. But the record also says she was nominated four times, three as the target, and took eight eviction votes. By Week 14, the remaining players could see that Jane had friends but not the numbers. Joel and Jules made the clean decision to evict her 2–0 over Tobias.
keyMoments: Week 4: enters the game as her own houseguest after the twins twist resolves
Week 7: is evicted 5–4, then later wins the Battle Back in Week 8
Week 10: survives against Ireland when the house unanimously removes Ireland
Week 12: wins veto and pulls Joel off the block
Week 12: votes out Felipe despite a final two with him
Week 14: is nominated beside Tobias and evicted 2–0
placements.resume: Jane could argue she came back into a house that had already voted her out, rebuilt working relationships, won HOH and veto, saved Joel, and repeatedly positioned herself as the vote people needed.
placements.demise: Joel and Jules ended Jane. Misha’s HOH placed Jane beside Tobias, and once Misha kept the veto unused, Joel gathered the two votes needed to remove Jane as the less useful endgame piece.
placements.optimalLine: Jane needed to force the Joel/Jules divide before final five instead of relying on Tobias and Joel as parallel shields. Once those two votes aligned, her pitch had no path.

placements.name: Aaron
placements.notes: Aaron was loyal, clutch, and respected, but his game narrowed too much and collapsed when he finally needed votes outside his core.
placements.story: Aaron’s game was more active than the finish suggests. He was nominated repeatedly, won important Block Busters and a veto, and stayed aligned with the house at an 89% rate. His loyalty to Tobias and later overlap with Felipe gave him structure, but it also made his path predictable. He was useful as a number and dangerous as a competitor, especially after saving himself multiple times. The fatal flaw was social range: when he reached the double eviction endgame, he did not have enough independent relationships to survive the replacement seat. Tobias flipping the final vote against him made the betrayal sting, but the groundwork was laid by weeks of playing tightly with the same people.
keyMoments: Week 5: wins veto while nominated and saves himself
Week 8: wins Block Buster to escape the block
Week 11: wins Block Buster again, forcing the Natasha/Tobias vote
Week 12: wins HOH and nominates Joel, Felipe and Jules
Week 13: wins Block Buster to escape the Jane/Gyselle vote
Week 13 double eviction: is renominated after Misha uses veto and evicted 2–1
placements.resume: Aaron could argue he won key safety comps under pressure, survived multiple target weeks, stayed loyal to his people, and took real shots when he finally had HOH.
placements.demise: Jane’s live HOH created the opening, Misha’s veto removed herself, and Tobias supplied the decisive betrayal. Aaron was evicted because Misha and Tobias decided Jules was more useful than Aaron at final six.
placements.optimalLine: Aaron needed to diversify earlier, especially with Misha and Jules. By the double, appealing to relationships he had not maintained was not enough.

placements.name: Gyselle
placements.notes: Gyselle was everywhere socially, but too often as the flexible piece other players used rather than the person directing the vote.
placements.story: Gyselle’s game had a real social footprint: five groups, eight people reached, and constant proximity to the season’s major structures. But her 70% voting alignment and three blindsides show the cost of playing between rooms without becoming the hub. She survived several blocks by winning two Block Busters and by letting bigger targets sit beside her. Her best moments were the Felipe vote and the way she could recruit Jane or Misha into temporary voting blocs. Her worst moments came when she assumed relationships would hold without confirming the numbers. Misha’s Week 13 HOH put her beside Jane and Joel, Joel used veto, Aaron hit the block, and the Drama Club numbers finally cut Gyselle loose.
keyMoments: Week 3: survives beside Amberly after the Power Couple protects her
Week 6: votes out Hasan despite their final two
Week 8: wins Block Buster and escapes the Aaron/Nico vote
Week 12: wins Block Buster and helps send Felipe out
Week 13: is renominated after Joel’s veto and fails to campaign hard enough
Week 13: is evicted 3–1 over Jane
placements.resume: Gyselle could argue she moved through multiple alliances, survived four nominations, won two Block Busters, and helped assemble the votes that removed Felipe.
placements.demise: Misha nominated Gyselle, Joel’s veto forced Aaron into the chair, and Tobias organized the 3–1 vote to evict Gyselle over Jane. The numbers were there before Gyselle fully accepted she was the target.
placements.optimalLine: Gyselle needed to own a side by Week 12. Floating had value, but at seven it left her without anyone willing to risk their game for her.

placements.name: Felipe
placements.notes: Felipe had one of the best alignment games in the cast, but no competition safety and too many exposed final twos left him vulnerable once the numbers got small.
placements.story: Felipe’s 90% voting alignment is the stat that defines him. For most of the season, he knew where the vote was going and was close enough to help decide whether to join it. He did this without HOH or veto power, which is a real social-strategic achievement. The downside was that his game depended on relationships staying private: Nico, Jules, Joel, Jane, and Aaron all occupied different versions of his endgame. Once those overlaps became visible, Felipe could not protect himself physically or rhetorically. At final eight, Jane and Misha moved with Gyselle to send him out 3–2, and he had no Block Buster win to rescue him.
keyMoments: Week 1: forms the Felipe/Nico final two
Week 2: adds a second final two with Jules
Week 5: helps recruit Joel into the Hasan vote
Week 8: betrays Nico in the 6–2 vote
Week 11: bonds with Joel and becomes visibly paired
Week 12: lands beside Jules after Gyselle wins Block Buster and is evicted 3–2
placements.resume: Felipe could argue he voted correctly 90% of the time, helped steer multiple majority votes without power, and built enough relationships that people kept giving him information even when they knew he had other deals.
placements.demise: Gyselle and Misha, with Jane as the decisive recruit, ended Felipe. Once Gyselle won Block Buster, Felipe was stuck beside Jules, and the War Room side saw him as the cleaner cut.
placements.optimalLine: Felipe needed to win one safety comp or consolidate around Joel earlier. Without that, the multiple final twos became evidence against him instead of insurance.

placements.name: Natasha
placements.notes: Natasha had social influence and loyalty, but her game became too visible as a pair-and-structure player to survive a tie vote.
placements.story: Natasha was central early through Zella, Gyselle, and the Power Couple, and she was often better socially than people credited. Her problem was that her loyalty was readable. Once Zella left, Natasha stayed connected but lost the shield that made her choices look less coordinated. She survived several weeks because bigger competitors and messier targets drew attention first. At Week 11, Joel nominated Natasha, Aaron and Tobias, and after Aaron saved himself in the Block Buster, Natasha sat beside Tobias in a vote that split exactly down the middle. Joel broke the tie against her, proving that her relationships were not enough when the HOH had a strategic preference.
keyMoments: Week 1: forms The Power Couple with Gyselle
Week 3: formalizes the Zella showmance and helps protect Gyselle
Week 5: votes out Hasan despite broader alliance ties
Week 10: wins Block Buster and escapes the Jane/Ireland vote
Week 11: sits beside Tobias after Aaron wins Block Buster
Week 11: is evicted on Joel’s tie-breaking vote
placements.resume: Natasha could argue she built durable bonds, helped shape early majority structures, won safety when she needed it in Week 10, and forced the house to split evenly before Joel broke the tie.
placements.demise: Joel ended Natasha. Gyselle, Jules and Misha voted to keep her, but Aaron, Felipe and Jane forced the tie, and Joel chose to evict Natasha as the more connected future problem.
placements.optimalLine: Natasha needed to cut away from Gyselle and Jane earlier or win veto in Week 11. At the time, loyalty was understandable, but it left her too easy to map.

placements.name: Ireland
placements.notes: Ireland was the season’s biggest comp force, but she was so rarely in the vote room that her safety wins became proof she had no stable path.
placements.story: Ireland’s raw numbers are absurd: three HOHs, four vetoes, three Block Busters, and repeated wins while targeted. But her 40% voting alignment is just as important. She was powerful, but not integrated; she kept surviving votes the house wanted to have without her. The Interrogation power bought her an early secret HOH, and her midgame veto streak made her feel inevitable for a while. The problem was that every win narrowed the house’s patience. Once Natasha beat her in the Week 10 Block Buster, Ireland lost the only thing keeping the room from acting unanimously, and every remaining voter wrote her name down.
keyMoments: Week 2: uses The Interrogation to take Nico’s HOH in secret
Week 3: wins Block Buster and escapes the Amberly/Gyselle vote
Week 4: wins Block Buster again and escapes the Harriett/Natasha vote
Week 6: wins HOH and veto, leaving Hasan and Tobias nominated
Week 8: wins veto and forces Nico onto Dylon’s block
Week 9: wins HOH and veto, removing Dylon unanimously
Week 10: loses Block Buster to Natasha and is evicted 7–0
placements.resume: Ireland could argue she won her way out of danger over and over, used an early secret power to seize HOH, and forced the house to spend multiple weeks failing to remove her.
placements.demise: Jules’s HOH put Ireland back in the danger structure, Misha’s veto changed the block, and Natasha’s Block Buster win took away Ireland’s last escape. After that, the seven voters did the obvious thing and removed the biggest comp threat.
placements.optimalLine: Ireland needed to use one of her HOHs to build a real majority instead of proving she could survive without one. Once the house saw her as a repeat comp problem, the correct play was earlier reconciliation, not louder targeting.

placements.name: Dylon
placements.notes: Dylon played hard and won power, but his game became too visible, too comp-dependent, and too easy to unite against.
placements.story: Dylon’s first half was very strong: two HOHs, a veto, and a secret Mystery Veto that saved him when the block looked settled. He had real reads and often identified structures before other people said them out loud. But he also overplayed suspicion into public accusations, and his alliances started treating him as the crack rather than the core. The Week 8 HOH bought him power but made him the obvious next target. When Ireland nominated Aaron, Tobias and Dylon in Week 9, Tobias won Block Buster and Dylon was left beside Aaron. The entire house recognized that Dylon was more dangerous if spared, and the vote became unanimous.
keyMoments: Week 1: wins the Mystery Veto instead of the HOH path
Week 5: wins HOH and nominates Ireland, Aaron and Zella
Week 6: uses the Mystery Veto after the ceremony and forces Nico onto the block
Week 8: wins HOH and targets Ireland, only for Ireland to veto herself
Week 8: sees Nico leave after the renom
Week 9: is nominated by Ireland and loses Block Buster to Tobias
Week 9: is evicted 8–0 over Aaron
placements.resume: Dylon could argue he won multiple powers, made major nominations, used the Mystery Veto to save himself, identified hidden voting blocs, and forced the house to treat him as a central threat.
placements.demise: Ireland nominated Dylon, but Tobias and the whole house ended him. Once Tobias won Block Buster, Dylon sat beside Aaron and every voter chose the cleaner comp-threat removal.
placements.optimalLine: Dylon needed to keep his reads private and let others take the shot at Ireland and the blocs. The information was often right; the delivery made him the move.

placements.name: Nico
placements.notes: Nico’s calm, loyal game kept him safe for a while, but waiting for other people to move left him exposed when Dylon needed a replacement target.
placements.story: Nico had a useful low-temperature game early, anchored by Felipe and a few timely safety results. His Week 2 HOH was stolen by Ireland’s power, which hurt his early agency and public perception. He was often trusted personally, but he did not convert that trust into control; a 67% voting alignment and one blindside show he was adjacent rather than central. His Block Buster win in Week 6 saved him, but in Week 8 the same comp-danger logic made him a replacement nominee. He did not campaign hard because he believed the number was there. It was not: Felipe, Misha, Jules, Tobias, Natasha and Ireland moved against him.
keyMoments: Week 2: wins HOH before Ireland secretly takes it through The Interrogation
Week 2: agrees to the Felipe final two that defines his early game
Week 6: wins Block Buster and escapes the Hasan/Tobias vote
Week 8: is renominated after Ireland uses veto
Week 8: does not campaign aggressively, trusting the count
Week 8: is evicted 6–2 and becomes the first juror
placements.resume: Nico could argue he built real trust, stayed calm under pressure, won safety when he needed it once, and kept his word in a house where that became rare.
placements.demise: Dylon named Nico as the replacement after Ireland used veto. The vote flipped away from Nico when Felipe and Tobias chose game over loyalty, and Nico’s lack of active campaigning gave the new majority room to settle.
placements.optimalLine: Nico needed to start the anti-Aaron or anti-Dylon move himself before he touched the block. Waiting for the room to protect him was the mistake he could have seen at the time.

placements.name: Hasan
placements.notes: Hasan’s early HOH made him look like a strategist, but he never rebuilt once his alliance map became visible.
placements.story: Hasan’s Week 3 HOH gave him real early influence, especially through Misha and the Power Couple. The problem is that the structure around him became public and brittle almost immediately. He nominated Amberly, Gyselle and Ireland, but the week did not produce the stable control he needed. By Week 5 he was a replacement nominee beside Zella, and the house used that chair to break up a known connection. His social ties with Gyselle and Misha were real, but not resilient enough. When Ireland won safety in the Block Buster, Hasan no longer had the bigger target beside him and was gone soon after, though the official boot order records him pre-jury.
keyMoments: Week 3: wins HOH and nominates Amberly, Gyselle and Ireland
Week 3: asks Gyselle to sit as a pawn, creating long-term distrust
Week 3: sees Amberly expose the Power Couple structure on the way out
Week 5: is renominated after Aaron uses veto
Week 5: survives the initial vote only because Zella leaves 6–5
Week 6: is nominated again by Ireland and evicted 9–1
placements.resume: Hasan could argue he won an early HOH, formed meaningful bonds with Misha and Gyselle, and correctly identified several threats before the house was ready to act.
placements.demise: Ireland’s Week 6 HOH put Hasan back on the block, Dylon’s Mystery Veto changed the shape but not the target pool, and the house chose Hasan over Tobias because Hasan’s alliance baggage was easier to punish.
placements.optimalLine: Hasan needed to repair with non-Power Couple players immediately after Amberly’s exit. Staying inside the same conversations made every later pitch sound self-interested.

placements.name: Zella
placements.notes: Zella played loudly, loyally and visibly, which made her useful early and cuttable the first time her allies needed a sacrifice.
placements.story: Zella had more influence than a pre-jury exit normally gets credited for. Her bond with Natasha shaped early voting blocs, and her Week 2 Block Buster win saved her from becoming an early casualty. But she was always visible: the showmance, the fights with Ireland, and her role in the Power Couple made her an easy symbol of a larger group. In Week 5, Dylon’s HOH put her on the block with Ireland and Aaron, then Aaron’s veto brought Hasan into the chair. Once Ireland won the Block Buster, the house had to choose between Zella and Hasan. Misha, Gyselle, Jane, Tobias, Jules and Joel landed on Zella, making her the casualty of a fractured alliance war.
keyMoments: Week 2: is renominated and wins Block Buster to save herself
Week 3: formalizes the Natasha showmance
Week 5: is nominated by Dylon beside Ireland and Aaron
Week 5: watches Aaron win veto and Hasan enter as renom
Week 5: loses Block Buster to Ireland
Week 5: is evicted 6–5 and exposes Misha on the way out
placements.resume: Zella could argue she won safety when nominated, protected Natasha even when it hurt her game, and was influential enough that people evicted her to weaken a structure rather than because she was irrelevant.
placements.demise: Misha’s side of the vote ended Zella. Once Ireland won Block Buster, Zella sat beside Hasan, and the anti-showmance and anti-Power Couple numbers converged by one vote.
placements.optimalLine: Zella needed to separate strategically from Natasha before the house forced the question. Loyalty was understandable, but the pair made her a target before she had enough independent numbers.

placements.name: Harriett
placements.notes: Harriett’s twin twist bought entry for Jane, but Harriett’s own game became too loud, too contradictory, and too easy to unite against.
placements.story: Harriett had an interesting opening because the twin twist gave her and Jane a unique structural advantage. But Harriett did not translate that advantage into trust. She was constantly in conversations, but the stories changed depending on the room, and by Week 4 too many people could compare notes. The Mystery Competitor power looked splashy but did not save her; Scott losing simply made the power a curiosity rather than a shield. Once Jules won HOH and nominated Harriett, Natasha and Ireland, Harriett’s contradictions became the easiest house consensus of the season. Ireland saved herself in the Block Buster, and Harriett left 12–0 over Natasha.
keyMoments: Week 1: enters as part of the secret twin twist
Week 2: forms The Pipeline with Stella, then votes against the alliance’s interest
Week 4: Jane enters as a separate houseguest, changing Harriett’s threat profile
Week 4: uses the Mystery Competitor power but gains no real safety
Week 4: is exposed by multiple conflicting stories
Week 4: is evicted unanimously over Natasha
placements.resume: Harriett could argue she helped survive the twin twist long enough to bring Jane into the game, won a secret power, and made enough deals that the house had to compare notes to catch her.
placements.demise: Jules nominated Harriett, and Misha, Dylon, Felipe and others exposed the contradictions in her pitches. Once Ireland won Block Buster, the vote against Harriett became the one thing every room could agree on.
placements.optimalLine: Harriett needed fewer stories and a cleaner target. After Jane entered, the correct move was to become boring for two weeks, not busier.

placements.name: Amberly
placements.notes: Amberly had real social instincts but never gained enough structural protection to survive once the Power Couple needed a clean early boot.
placements.story: Amberly was more socially aware than the house gave her credit for. She spotted the shape of the Power Couple and named it accurately on the way out. The issue is that she lacked a stable alliance seat before she needed one. Hasan’s HOH put her on the block beside Gyselle and Ireland, and Dylon’s veto not being used left her exposed. Ireland winning Block Buster removed the obvious comp threat from the vote and reduced the decision to Amberly versus Gyselle. The larger group protected Gyselle, and Amberly left with information the house only believed after it was too late for her.
keyMoments: Week 1: bonds broadly but fails to find a real plan
Week 2: is protected by Ireland’s secret HOH deal but remains outside the main structure
Week 3: is nominated by Hasan as the target
Week 3: correctly identifies the Power Couple as the house’s hidden bloc
Week 3: loses Block Buster to Ireland
Week 3: is evicted 10–2 over Gyselle
placements.resume: Amberly could argue she read the house correctly, exposed the Power Couple, and campaigned against a real structure rather than chasing personal grudges.
placements.demise: Hasan nominated Amberly, but the Power Couple and its satellites ended her. Once Ireland saved herself, Natasha, Zella, Felipe, Misha and enough free agents protected Gyselle and made Amberly the easy vote.
placements.optimalLine: Amberly needed to lock a counter-alliance before saying the structure out loud. The read was right; the timing left her with information and no votes.

placements.name: Stella
placements.notes: Stella’s loyalty was genuine, but she had no backup plan once the first real vote moved away from her.
placements.story: Stella never got the runway to build a full game. She was loyal to Harriett and connected enough to matter socially, but not enough to command votes. Ireland’s Week 2 secret HOH put Stella beside Jules and Joel, and Joel’s veto removed the most obvious third option. Zella won Block Buster, leaving Stella against Jules. Stella believed the count was closer than it was, which tells the whole story: people were kind to her but not voting for her. Tobias voting against her despite an early deal underlined how little leverage she had.
keyMoments: Week 1: connects with Jules and Harriett but does not enter a durable majority
Week 2: is nominated by Ireland
Week 2: forms The Pipeline with Harriett
Week 2: loses Block Buster to Zella
Week 2: is evicted 10–3 over Jules
Week 8: loses the first Battle Back round to Amberly
placements.resume: Stella’s honest case is loyalty: she built real bonds, kept faith with Harriett, and tried to argue that keeping her gave people a reliable vote. She did not have a strategic résumé beyond that.
placements.demise: Ireland’s nominations put Stella in danger, Joel’s veto preserved Jules as the comparison, and the house chose to keep Jules as the more useful player. The 10 votes were there before Stella realized the room had closed.
placements.optimalLine: Stella needed to campaign earlier and against Jules specifically, not rely on loyalty being recognized. Given how little game had formed, though, her ceiling was always low.

twists.name: No Eviction
twists.desc: No nomination ceremony, no veto and no vote: the house is the same size on Thursday as it was on Sunday. The Head of Household competition still runs and still crowns somebody, which leaves one houseguest holding the most powerful seat in the game with absolutely nothing to spend it on — and everybody else with a week to work in and no ceremony to be judged by. Pairs with anything hiding inside the competition, because a week that cannot evict anybody is a week whose only outcome is who walked away holding something.

twists.name: Secret Power Competition
twists.desc: Three powers are hidden inside this week's Head of Household competition, and before a single houseguest plays they decide in private what they are actually competing for: the crown, or one of the three. Not both. The outgoing Head of Household cannot win the crown back and so plays only for a power, which is the one week their exclusion is worth something. Somebody out there is about to post the best score of the afternoon and not be Head of Household, because that was never what they were running for — and the house will spend weeks not understanding why. Winners are told alone and nothing is announced. Every power won here dies the moment the jury opens, which is why they are allowed to be this strong.

twists.name: Have-Nots
twists.desc: The new Head of Household puts part of the house on slop, cold showers and the have-not room for the week. Have-nots compete at a real disadvantage in the veto, and nobody forgets who chose them.

twists.name: The Twin Twist
twists.desc: One houseguest was secretly two people swapping places every week. Harriett and Jane played as one, and lasted long enough to both enter the game as individuals in week 4.

twists.name: Prizes and Punishments
twists.desc: The veto competition stops awarding the veto and starts deciding who picks first. Everybody then chooses a wrapped box: the Power of Veto is in one of them, and the rest hold cash, a holiday, a call home, a bag of confetti, or a punishment nobody wants. Finish last in the competition and you pick first, blind; win it and you pick last, with every opened box on the table and stealable. Anything stolen once is frozen and can never be taken again, so the veto changes hands in public until somebody makes it stop — and every season this format runs, somebody on the block chooses the money.

twists.name: Something In This House
twists.desc: A real power is hidden somewhere in the house — behind the cereal, under a have-not bed, in the HOH cistern — and the house is told only that it exists. No clue, no competition, no map. The only way to hold it is to go and look, and looking is not a private act: a houseguest seen rummaging is a houseguest who visibly believes there is something to find, which costs them and makes everybody else start looking too. Whoever finds it is told nothing publicly. If nobody finds it in four evictions it is taken away and the house never learns it was there.

twists.name: Battle Back
twists.desc: The evicted houseguests are not gone. After this week's eviction they compete for the right to walk back in — as a gauntlet, where the first evictee must beat every person who followed them out, or as a Showdown, where the survivor still has to get past a champion the house elects to hold the door shut. The winner re-enters with no immunity and a complete memory of who voted them out.

twists.name: Double Eviction
twists.desc: Two evictions in one night. The week plays normally, and the moment the first houseguest walks out the house runs a second, compressed cycle live: new Head of Household, nominations, veto and vote with no time to campaign properly. Two people leave.

seasonNarrative: Season 1 was defined by a simple fact: the plan held only five times and broke ten. This was not a steamroll; it was a room constantly re-deciding itself. Early power structures like The Power Couple, The Dock Pact, The Oath and The War Room looked solid until one vote exposed the cracks. Comp threats like Ireland and Dylon forced the house to spend weeks solving immediate survival problems, while social players like Misha, Jules, Tobias and Jane made those solutions possible. The jury rewarded the player who best combined both modes. Misha did not dominate every week, but she was present in enough rooms, saved by enough relationships, and clutch in enough late competitions to win 5–4.

bestStrategic.name: Misha
bestStrategic.description: Misha’s strategy was adaptable rather than linear: she moved through collapsing structures, kept herself worth saving, and cut Joel at the exact moment his résumé became fatal to her.

bestSocial.name: Jules
bestSocial.description: Jules was the season’s best pure social player, repeatedly surviving target weeks because people felt heard by him even when they were not aligned with him.

bestPhysical.name: Ireland
bestPhysical.description: Ireland’s combined HOH, veto and Block Buster run made her the clearest physical and competition force of the season.

mostClutch.name: Misha
mostClutch.description: Misha won three times under threat, including the final-four veto and the final HOH sequence that let her choose the winning endgame.

mostLoyal.name: Aaron
mostLoyal.description: Aaron’s loyalty to Tobias and his core was not always optimal, but it was consistent enough that even people who cut him understood what kind of game he was trying to play.

bestUnderdog.name: Jane
bestUnderdog.description: Jane entered late, was evicted, fought back in, and still became a real late-game player rather than a novelty returnee.

biggestVillain.name: Misha
biggestVillain.description: Misha owned enough hidden votes and late cuts that the jury often had to respect her through resentment.

mostChaotic.name: Ireland
mostChaotic.description: Ireland combined secret power, repeated comp wins, public feuds, and a 40% voting alignment into the most volatile game in the house.

quietestThreat.name: Felipe
quietestThreat.description: Felipe had no HOH or veto wins, but a 90% voting alignment and constant endgame deals made him far more dangerous than his résumé looked.

seasonMVP.name: Misha
seasonMVP.description: Misha is the MVP because the season’s deciding arc is hers: survive the middle, win the end, and choose the opponent.

mostTragic.name: Joel
mostTragic.description: Joel was one question and one decision from the final two, then had to vote for the person who cut him.

mostUnlucky.name: Jane
mostUnlucky.description: Jane survived a brutal path back into the house only to be trapped at final five by a clean 2–0 vote she could not meaningfully disrupt.

ironPerson.name: Tobias
ironPerson.description: Tobias lasted 15 weeks, survived five nominations, and remained socially relevant almost to the end despite being used as a pawn repeatedly.

biggestMeltdown.name: Dylon
biggestMeltdown.description: Dylon’s public exposure of The War Room and his escalating feud with Ireland turned correct reads into reasons to evict him.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Misha gets gold for winning with the best blend of social insulation, late comps and final decision-making.

silver.name: Jules
silver.description: Jules gets silver for a finalist game that came within one vote and had real influence across the season.

gold.name: Tobias
gold.description: Tobias became the audience favorite because even when he betrayed people, he tended to make the house feel human.

silver.name: Aaron
silver.description: Aaron’s loyalty, clutch saves and straightforward emotional game gave the season a grounded counterweight to the chaos.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Misha’s winning game included hidden votes, strategic denials and the final Joel cut, making her the season’s most effective villain.

silver.name: Ireland
silver.description: Ireland’s public feuds, secret HOH and relentless comp safety made her the antagonist of multiple rooms.

gold.name: Ireland
gold.description: Ten total safety or power wins made Ireland the season’s clear competition monster.

silver.name: Misha
silver.description: Misha’s six HOH/veto wins mattered most late, when every competition directly shaped the endgame.

gold.name: Jules
gold.description: Jules used conversation as protection and reached finale night because people kept wanting him in their endgame.

silver.name: Tobias
silver.description: Tobias’s group reach and nomination survival show a social game that kept working even when his name was on the block.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Misha’s strategic edge was timing: she rarely overclaimed early and took full ownership only when the game required it.

silver.name: Jules
silver.description: Jules read rooms well, especially on HOH weeks, but lost points for not making the jury see enough direct ownership.

gold.name: Joel
gold.description: Joel lost the final HOH tiebreaker, watched Misha choose Jules, and became the last juror one decision from the prize.

silver.name: Tobias
silver.description: Tobias was evicted 1–0 by Misha after believing enough of the relationship to be hurt by the cut.

gold.name: Ireland
gold.description: Ireland’s Interrogation power created a secret HOH and set the template for the season’s hidden-power paranoia.

silver.name: Dylon
silver.description: Dylon’s Mystery Veto saved him after the veto ceremony and changed an already-settled block.

gold.name: Joel
gold.description: Joel had a winning argument if he reached the final two, but Misha correctly cut him before the jury could reward it.

gold.name: Misha
gold.description: Misha’s final tribal-style questioning was uneven, but her closing statement and ownership at the reunion gave enough jurors permission to vote for the better overall game.

gold.name: Jules
gold.description: Losing 5–4 makes Jules the obvious robbed finalist: he had the social case, several jurors defending him, and still fell one vote short.

messiestFeud.description: Dylon and Ireland turned promises, powers, false stories and public callouts into the season’s longest-running strategic grudge.

biggestBetrayal.description: Misha cut Joel at final three despite his expectation that the final decision could still favor him, choosing the only opponent she could beat.

secondBiggestBetrayal.description: Jane voted out Felipe after a final two, turning one of her key bonds into the vote that sent him to jury.

legacyMoment.name: Misha chooses Jules over Joel
legacyMoment.description: The season’s defining move was Misha winning the final HOH and cutting Joel, converting a near-certain losing final two into a 5–4 victory.

fanFavorite.name: Tobias
fanFavorite.description: Tobias was voted the house's favourite by the audience.
